paper.title:
Where Does Toxicity Live? Mechanistic Localization
and Targeted Suppression in Language Models WARNING: The content contains offensive model outputs and is toxic.
paper.abstract: Abstract Large language models frequently generate toxic, hateful, or harmful content, yet existing mitigation methods rely on costly retraining or output-level filtering with no mechanistic insight into where toxicity originates internally. We introduce Meow2X and TRNE , two complementary retraining-free frameworks that localize toxicity to specific layers and neurons by analyzing activation differentials between toxic and neutral prompts, then suppress them via inference-time scaling or minimal rank-one weight edits—without any gradient descent. Evaluations across five LMs, two benchmarks, and 90 configurations using dual safety evaluators demonstrate consistent toxicity reduction while preserving language modeling quality. Our analysis reveals that toxicity is disproportionately encoded in early MLP layers, varies across architectures, and is systematically underestimated by single-evaluator setups—underscoring the need for multi-evaluator safety assessment. By bridging mechanistic interpretability with practical detoxification, our framework offers a principled path toward safer, more transparent language models. sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across various downstream tasks; however, their propensity to generate toxic, hateful, or harmful content remains a significant challenge for real-world deployment ( Sap et al., 2019a ; Gehman et al., 2020 ; Dementieva et al., 2025 ; Welbl et al., 2021 ; Hui et al., 2024 ) . Existing safety mechanisms—including instruction tuning, RLHF, and adversarial fine-tuning—typically require expensive retraining or exhibit limited transfer to out-of-distribution inputs ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Beniwal et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . We address this with two complementary post-hoc methods that localize and suppress toxic neural components without retraining, exploiting the observation that toxicity correlates with specific activation patterns in attention and MLP modules ( Meng et al., 2022 ; Zhang and Nanda, 2023 ; Costa-jussà et al., 2024 ; Shaik et al., 2025 ) . Figure 1: Overview of the Meow2X framework. Given toxic and neutral prompts, the model identifies toxic layers (attn-5, MLP-17) via activation differentials. Three inference-time suppression strategies reduce toxic generation while preserving neutral outputs, without any parameter updates.

sections.heading: Research Gap
sections.text: Prior work has identified toxic neurons and suppressed them ( Suau et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) , but typically targets individual neurons or fixed concepts without systematically selecting layers per model and dataset ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zhao and Huang, 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025b ) . Most methods also apply generic damping rather than interventions tailored to the difference between toxic and neutral inputs ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Villate-Castillo et al., 2024 ; Pozzobon et al., 2024 ; Siu et al., 2025 ) . There is no simple, data-driven algorithm that (1) detects which layers are most correlated with toxicity and (2) suppresses them while tracking output quality ( Koh et al., 2024 ; Suau et al., 2024 ) . We fill this gap with Meow2X ( M echanistic E xploration o f W eight-level To x icity), a parameter-frozen inference-time framework based on activation differentials, and TRNE ( T oxicity R eduction via N euron E diting), a lightweight rank-one weight update guided by contrastive gradient localization.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.text: Both methods share the insight that only a small fraction of layers govern toxic behavior ( Lee et al., 2025 ) . As shown in Figure 1 , Meow2X identifies these layers via mean activation differences between toxic and neutral inputs and suppresses them at inference time via scaling—leaving weights unchanged and the intervention fully reversible ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Shaik et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . TRNE localizes the same layers via contrastive gradient norms and commits a minimal, norm-constrained rank-one weight edit that encodes the toxic direction directly into the projection matrix—offering a persistent correction without gradient descent. Together, they combine interpretability (knowing where toxicity arises) with effectiveness (measured by safety classifiers) ( Neplenbroek et al., 2024 ; Jain et al., 2024 ) , grounded in mechanistic interpretability findings that toxic behaviors are mediated by localized neuron-level circuits ( Olah et al., 2020 ; Meng et al., 2022 ; Geiger et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., ) .

sections.heading: Contributions
sections.text: Our contributions are threefold: • A principled toxic layer detection framework using activation differentials ( Meow2X ) and contrastive gradient norms ( TRNE ), revealing where toxicity is encoded in language models. • A controlled evaluation across 90 configurations —five LLMs, two datasets, three component scopes, three intervention strategies—without any parameter updates for Meow2X and with minimal rank-one edits for TRNE . • A model-agnostic detoxification pipeline that preserves language modeling capability via reversible inference-time scaling ( Meow2X ) or norm-constrained weight editing ( TRNE ). sections.heading: Detoxification of Language Models.
sections.text: Prior work on toxicity mitigation in language models has largely focused on training-time interventions, including supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning from human feedback, as well as on output-level filtering and rejection sampling ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Beniwal et al., 2025 ; Sap et al., 2019b ) . While effective at reducing harmful generations, these approaches treat toxicity as a surface-level behavior and provide limited insight into how such behaviors arise internally ( Dathathri et al., 2019 ) . Moreover, they typically require retraining or additional inference-time classifiers ( Costa-jussà et al., 2024 ) . In contrast, our work operates directly on internal representations and performs targeted inference-time interventions without modifying model parameters.

sections.heading: Interpretability via Internal Representations.
sections.text: Mechanistic interpretability research has shown that neural behaviors can often be localized to specific layers, neurons, or substructures ( Zhang and Nanda, 2023 ) . Methods such as Network Dissection ( Bau et al., 2017 ) and representational similarity analysis ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) demonstrate that internal activations encode semantically meaningful features and that behaviors can be traced to localized components. These findings motivate our approach, which explicitly compares mean activations induced by toxic and neutral inputs to identify layers and neurons that disproportionately contribute to toxic behavior ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Siu et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Targeted and Causal Interventions.
sections.text: Recent studies have explored the causal manipulation of internal components through neuron ablation, attention head suppression, or feature scaling, demonstrating that selective intervention can reliably alter model outputs ( Li and Janson, 2024 ; Dai et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . However, many such approaches rely on manual selection or task-specific heuristics. Our method systematizes this process by using activation differentials and contribution-based scoring to automatically identify toxic layers and apply controlled scaling through forward hooks, enabling reproducible and architecture-agnostic intervention ( Rai et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Evaluation and Positioning.
sections.text: Unlike prior detoxification methods that rely on a single evaluator or aggregate metrics, our framework employs multiple independent safety classifiers and jointly measures toxicity reduction and language modeling quality ( Yang et al., 2025a ; Dutta, 2024 ) . Overall, our work bridges safety and interpretability by framing toxicity as an internal representational phenomenon ( Suau et al., 2024 ) . Rather than only suppressing harmful outputs, we focus on revealing where toxicity is encoded within the model, providing both practical mitigation and mechanistic insight into models.

sections.heading: Positioning Against Baselines.
sections.text: We position our work relative to the closest prior methods: Whispering Experts Suau et al. (2024) suppresses toxic neurons but requires task-specific expert identification and does not generalize across architectures without per-model re-identification. SafeEdit Wang et al. (2024) applies knowledge editing via gradient-based updates but requires backpropagation at inference time. DExperts Liu et al. (2021) and PPLM Dathathri et al. (2020) are output-level steering methods that cannot localize toxicity to specific model components. Unlike all of the above, Meow2X operates without any parameter updates, backpropagation, or expert model, making it strictly lighter at inference time. A full quantitative comparison is left to future work as it requires standardizing generation hyperparameters, decoding strategies, and evaluation prompts across codebases—a non-trivial engineering challenge acknowledged by prior surveys Villate-Castillo et al. (2024) .

sections.heading: 3 Methodology - Meow2X
sections.text: As highlighted in Algorithm 1 , we explain the operations as:

sections.heading: 3.1 Toxic Layer Detection
sections.text: We identify toxic layers by analyzing systematic differences in internal activations elicited by toxic and neutral inputs. Given a pretrained language model M M with L L model layers, we focus on either attention blocks, MLP blocks, or both, depending on the experimental setting.

sections.heading: Activation Collection.
sections.text: Let 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} and 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}_{n} denote sets of toxic and neutral prompts, respectively. For each layer ℓ \ell , we collect mean activation vectors by registering forward hooks during inference and averaging hidden states across tokens and batch samples. We compute separate mean activations for toxic inputs μ t ℓ \mu_{t}^{\ell} and neutral inputs μ n ℓ \mu_{n}^{\ell} using batched forward passes to ensure stable estimates.

sections.heading: Activation Differentials and Layer Scoring.
sections.text: To quantify toxicity-specific behavior, we compute the activation differential Δ ℓ = μ t ℓ − μ n ℓ \Delta^{\ell}=\mu_{t}^{\ell}-\mu_{n}^{\ell} for each layer. We assign a scalar toxicity score to each layer by aggregating absolute differences across neurons, S ℓ = ‖ Δ ℓ ‖ 1 , S^{\ell}=\|\Delta^{\ell}\|_{1}, where higher values indicate stronger representational divergence induced by toxic prompts. This score provides a coarse but robust signal for ranking layers by toxicity relevance.

sections.heading: Neuron-Level Contribution Analysis.
sections.text: Beyond layer-level scoring, we estimate the concentration of toxicity within a layer. For each Δ ℓ \Delta^{\ell} , we identify toxic neurons as those whose absolute activation difference exceeds the 90 th 90^{\text{th}} percentile. We then compute a contribution ratio c ℓ = ∑ i ∈ 𝒯 ℓ | Δ i ℓ | ∑ i | Δ i ℓ | , c^{\ell}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}_{\ell}}|\Delta^{\ell}_{i}|}{\sum_{i}|\Delta^{\ell}_{i}|}, where 𝒯 ℓ \mathcal{T}_{\ell} denotes the set of toxic neurons in layer ℓ \ell . This captures whether toxicity arises from a small subset of highly influential neurons or is diffusely distributed.

sections.heading: Layer Selection.
sections.text: We select toxic layers using either a Top- k k strategy, which chooses the k k layers with the highest S ℓ S^{\ell} , or a dynamic thresholding strategy. In the latter, layers are selected if their score exceeds a data-dependent threshold defined by the mean and standard deviation of { S ℓ } \{S^{\ell}\} , with safeguards in place to enforce minimum and maximum numbers of selected layers. Both strategies operate identically across model architectures and component types.

sections.heading: Outputs.
sections.text: The detector returns (i) the set of selected toxic layers, (ii) layer-wise toxicity scores S ℓ S^{\ell} , and (iii) neuron-level contribution statistics c ℓ c^{\ell} . These signals are subsequently used to guide targeted inference-time interventions while preserving the original model parameters.

sections.heading: Mitigation Strategies.
sections.text: Following toxic layer identification, we intervene directly at inference time by modifying intermediate activations of selected model components. Let ℒ \mathcal{L} denote the set of detected toxic layers. For each layer ℓ ∈ ℒ \ell\in\mathcal{L} , we register forward hooks that rescale the output activations of either the attention block, the MLP block, or both, depending on the experimental setting. These interventions are lightweight, do not alter model parameters, and can be removed after generation.

sections.heading: 3.2.1 Deactivation
sections.text: The deactivation strategy applies uniform suppression to all selected layers. For each ℓ ∈ ℒ \ell\in\mathcal{L} , the layer output is multiplied by a constant scaling factor α = 1 − s \alpha=1-s , where s ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] s\in(0,1] is the deactivation strength. This strategy aggressively attenuates toxic representations by uniformly reducing their contribution to downstream layers. To avoid destabilizing the forward pass, the scaling factor is clipped to a minimum value α min \alpha_{\min} , ensuring that information flow is preserved.

sections.heading: 3.2.2 Dampening
sections.text: The dampening strategy performs moderate suppression by applying a reduced scaling factor relative to deactivation. Instead of fully applying the specified strength, activations are scaled by α = 1 − s 2 \alpha=1-\frac{s}{2} , resulting in a smoother attenuation of toxic signals. This strategy is particularly effective when toxicity is distributed across multiple layers and excessive suppression may harm fluency or coherence.

sections.heading: 3.2.3 Adaptive Scaling
sections.text: The adaptive strategy introduces contribution-aware suppression by conditioning the scaling factor on each layer’s estimated toxicity contribution. For a layer ℓ \ell , the scaling factor is computed as α ℓ = 1 − s ⋅ c ℓ max ℓ ′ ∈ ℒ ⁡ c ℓ ′ \alpha_{\ell}=1-s\cdot\frac{c_{\ell}}{\max_{\ell^{\prime}\in\mathcal{L}}c_{\ell^{\prime}}} , where c ℓ c_{\ell} denotes the normalized contribution score derived from high-magnitude activation differences. Layers with stronger toxic influence are thus suppressed more aggressively, while layers with weaker contributions remain largely intact. As with other strategies, α ℓ \alpha_{\ell} is lower-bounded by α min \alpha_{\min} to maintain numerical stability.

sections.heading: Practical Considerations
sections.text: All mitigation strategies are applied only during generation and are removed immediately afterward, preserving the original model for subsequent evaluations. The approach is fully model-agnostic, supports attention-only, MLP-only, or combined interventions, and integrates seamlessly with both top- k k and dynamic threshold–based layer selection. sections.heading: 4.1.1 Contrastive Gradient Localization
sections.text: For each input x x , we backpropagate through − ℒ ent ​ ( x ) -\mathcal{L}_{\text{ent}}(x) and register backward hooks on target modules to capture gradient norms. Layers where toxic inputs elicit substantially stronger gradients than neutral inputs are selected as toxic regions.

sections.heading: 4.1.2 Pre-Projection Activation Collection
sections.text: At each selected hotspot layer l l , we register forward hooks on the output projection (attention: o_proj ; MLP: down_proj ) to capture input activations at the last token position, ϕ l ​ ( x ) = h l ( last ) ​ ( x ) ∈ ℝ d in \phi_{l}(x)=h_{l}^{(\text{last})}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}} . Mean activations μ T \mu_{T} and μ N \mu_{N} are computed over the toxic and neutral sets respectively; the difference δ = μ T − μ N \delta=\mu_{T}-\mu_{N} defines the toxic direction at that layer.

sections.heading: 4.1.3 Rank-One Weight Update
sections.text: The key formula modifies the weight matrix: W new = W − α × torch.outer ​ ( δ , μ T ) ‖ μ T ‖ 2 + ϵ W_{\text{new}}=W-\alpha\times\frac{\texttt{torch.outer}(\delta,\mu_{T})}{\|\mu_{T}\|^{2}+\epsilon} This creates a “detector” ( μ T \mu_{T} ) and a “correction” ( δ \delta ). When future input looks toxic (similar to μ T \mu_{T} ), the matrix automatically subtracts the toxic direction. Neutral inputs (orthogonal to μ T \mu_{T} ) pass through unchanged. Analogy : Like calibrating a speaker system. You identify which frequencies cause distortion (localization), measure the distortion pattern (activation collection), then adjust the equalizer to cancel exactly that distortion without affecting clean frequencies (rank-one update).

sections.heading: 5.1 Dataset
sections.text: We evaluate our framework on two complementary toxicity benchmarks with distinct structural properties. We evaluate on: Real Toxicity Prompts (RTP) 2 2 2 https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/real-toxicity-prompts ( Gehman et al., 2020 ) and ParaDetox 3 3 3 https://huggingface.co/datasets/textdetox/multilingual_paradetox ( Logacheva et al., 2022 ; Dementieva et al., 2021 ) . Let 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} and 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}_{n} denote toxic and neutral prompt sets, respectively. For RTP, prompts with toxicity score τ ≥ 0.5 \tau\geq 0.5 are assigned to 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} , and the rest to 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}_{n} . ParaDetox provides paired samples ( x t , x n ) (x_{t},x_{n}) that differ primarily in toxicity while preserving semantics. We sample | 𝒟 t | = | 𝒟 n | = 2500 |\mathcal{D}_{t}|=|\mathcal{D}_{n}|=2500 , truncate inputs to 512 tokens, and cache all samples to ensure reproducibility. More details in Section § A.1 .

sections.heading: 5.2 Models
sections.text: Experiments are conducted on instruction-tuned causal language models M θ M_{\theta} in the 1B–3B parameter range, including Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct , gemma-2-2b-it , Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct , phi-2 , and TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 variants. Each model consists of a stack of layers { ℓ 1 , … , ℓ L } \{\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{L}\} , where each layer contains an attention block ℓ attn \ell^{\text{attn}} and an MLP block ℓ mlp \ell^{\text{mlp}} . The pipeline explicitly supports heterogeneous architectural layouts by dynamically identifying blocks across model families (e.g., model.layers, transformer.h, or attn.k). Our analysis is performed on attention-only, MLP-only, and combined components. All models are evaluated in inference mode using half-precision weights, without retraining or parameter updates, and batch sizes are tuned per model for stable activation collection.

sections.heading: 5.3 Toxicity Detection
sections.text: Toxicity is evaluated using two independent safety classifiers, Llama-Guard-3-8B ( Dubey et al., 2024 ) and PolyGuard-Qwen ( Kumar et al., 2025 ) . Given a prompt–response pair ( x , y ) (x,y) , each evaluator outputs a binary unsafe indicator u ∈ { 0 , 1 } u\in\{0,1\} and a set of violated safety categories 𝒞 ⊆ { S 1 , … , S 14 } \mathcal{C}\subseteq\{S_{1},\ldots,S_{14}\} . The categories cover violence, hate, sexual content, self-harm, privacy violations, and related safety risks. Using two heterogeneous evaluators enables robust verification of toxicity reductions across category boundaries. More details in Appendix A.1 .

sections.heading: 5.4 Metrics
sections.text: The effectiveness of detoxification is measured by comparing aggregate toxicity rates before and after mitigation. Let U before U_{\text{before}} and U after U_{\text{after}} denote the fraction of unsafe generations; toxicity reduction is defined as Δ ​ U = U before − U after \Delta U=U_{\text{before}}-U_{\text{after}} . Model utility is assessed via perplexity (PPL), computed using teacher-forced likelihood with attention-mask weighting. In addition, we report layer-level toxicity scores S ℓ S^{\ell} , neuron contribution ratios c ℓ c^{\ell} , and applied scaling factors α ℓ \alpha^{\ell} to analyze safety–utility trade-offs at a mechanistic level.

sections.heading: Meow2X
sections.text: Figures 2 – 4 jointly provide a multi-resolution view of how toxicity is encoded within Qwen-2.5 across layers, components, and neurons on the ParaDetox dataset. The neuron-level heatmaps (Figure 2 ) show that toxicity-related activation differences are sparse and structured rather than uniformly distributed (We observed different patterns in different models; see appendix § A.3 for more details), with particularly strong signals concentrated in the initial MLP layers (layers 1–5). This pattern is further corroborated by the layer-wise toxicity scores and contribution plots (Figure 3 ), where MLP components consistently exhibit higher toxicity scores S = ∥ Δ ∥ 1 S=\lVert\Delta\rVert_{1} than attention across both early and late layers, while attention contributions remain comparatively stable and lower in magnitude. The box plots and scatter analyses reveal a clear separation between MLP and attention components, indicating that toxicity is disproportionately encoded in feed-forward transformations. Finally, the neuron-level grids (Figure 4 ) demonstrate that within high-scoring MLP layers, toxicity is dominated by a small subset of neurons exhibiting large activation deviations beyond the percentile threshold. Collectively, these results indicate that toxicity in Qwen-2.5 emerges from localized neuron subspaces within specific MLP layers, motivating targeted, layer-wise inference-time interventions rather than global model modification. We observed similar patterns for the other models as well. Finding : Localizing toxicity is difficult — it varies across architectures, layers, and components, so precise localization is challenging.

sections.heading: TRNE
sections.text: Our experiments in Figures 17 , 18 , and 19 reveal that toxicity is not confined to a single component type. In TinyLlama, both attention layers [1, 2, 3, 4, 6] and MLP layers [0, 1, 2, 3, 5] exhibit elevated contrastive scores, with toxicity concentrated in early layers. In Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct in Figures 11 , 12 , and 13 , toxicity shifts to late layers, with attention [22, 21, 20, 23, 19] and MLP [21, 20, 22, 19, 23] showing similar distributions. This co-localization suggests that toxic circuits span both component types at consistent depths within each architecture. Notably, MLP editing consistently reduces toxicity (PolyGuard: − 6.4 -6.4 pp for TinyLlama, − 5.6 -5.6 pp for Llama-3.2-3B), while attention editing alone sometimes increases detected toxicity ( + 4.6 +4.6 pp and + 3.6 +3.6 pp respectively). This asymmetry indicates that MLP layers encode more direct toxic associations, whereas attention layers may contribute to contextual processing that, when disrupted, triggers refusal patterns classified as toxic by safety evaluators. Finding : Toxicity is distributed across both attention and MLP components at similar layer depths, not isolated to a single pathway.

sections.heading: (RQ2) Is layer deactivation an effective measure to mitigate toxicity?

From the comprehensive data, configuration (5,2) demonstrates the most reliable toxicity reduction with minimal fluency degradation—Gemma MLP achieves complete LG elimination (0.40% → \rightarrow 0.00%) and 3.4% PG reduction while PPL increases by merely 0.74 points. The (5,5) configuration proves effective for Llama3_2, achieving the highest single-model PG improvement (37.80% → \rightarrow 32.20%) at this moderate setting, though Phi-2 and Gemma exhibit PPL sensitivity. Configuration (10,2) yields the most substantial PG reduction overall, with Tiny-llama MLP dropping from 44.60% to 29.80% (14.8 percentage points) while maintaining acceptable PPL (+1.86). The (10,5) pair shows inconsistent results—Qwen-2 achieves decent toxicity reduction but PPL nearly doubles, indicating diminishing returns at higher layer counts. Most critically, the aggressive (10,20) configuration causes catastrophic model degradation across all architectures, with PPL values exploding to thousands (Llama3_2: 9297, Phi-2: 40060), rendering outputs incoherent despite apparent toxicity metric changes. These findings suggest that conservative edit strengths (2-5) targeting fewer layers preserve model utility while achieving meaningful safety improvements. sections.heading: (RQ3) Can model-agnostic, retraining-free interventions mitigate toxicity while preserving language quality?
sections.text: Table 2 shows that inference-time, retraining-free interventions consistently reduce toxicity across models and datasets while largely preserving language quality, as evidenced by small and stable changes in perplexity. Despite variation across architectures and components, toxicity mitigation is achieved without parameter updates, indicating that activation-level scaling is an effective and model-agnostic strategy. Configurations employing full deactivation on ParaDetox with Llama-3.2-3B exhibit PPL spikes (12.96 → \rightarrow 135.37), consistent with the observation that deactivation of structurally critical layers disrupts coherent generation; dampening and adaptive scaling reliably avoid this failure mode (PPL changes of < < 10 across all other configurations). Finding : Inference-time interventions reduce toxicity with minimal impact on language quality.

sections.heading: (RQ4) Is gradient update efficient to update the models?
sections.text: While TRNE achieves toxicity reduction on Llama-family models with moderate edit strength and few layers, aggressive hyperparameters can catastrophically degrade model quality. On Gemma-2-2B-it with high edit strength (20) and many layers (10), MLP editing caused perplexity to explode from 29.9 to 1744.6, rendering the model incoherent (As shown in Figures 14 , 15 , and 16 ). Simultaneously, toxicity increased by 21 percentage points on PolyGuard—the opposite of the intended effect. This fragility stems from the cumulative nature of weight updates: each layer modification compounds across multiple layers. When the total perturbation exceeds the model’s tolerance, coherent generation collapses. We recommend low-to-moderate edit strength (1 to 5) and editing only 3 to 5 layers as safe operating ranges, with architecture-specific tuning for non-Llama models. Finding : Weight editing is fragile—high edit strength or too many layers causes model collapse with perplexity exploding.

sections.heading: (RQ5) Safety Evaluators Measure Different Aspects of Model Behavior?
sections.text: LlamaGuard and PolyGuard produce dramatically different toxicity assessments on identical outputs. Baseline measurements differ by 25 to 40 percentage points, with PolyGuard consistently detecting far more toxic content. More critically, the evaluators disagree on the effect of attention editing: LlamaGuard reports improvement while PolyGuard reports degradation. This disagreement reveals that the evaluators measure fundamentally different phenomena. LlamaGuard focuses on explicitly harmful content generation, while PolyGuard additionally penalizes refusal behavior and evasive responses. When attention layers are edited, models may become more likely to refuse requests, which PolyGuard considers problematic, but LlamaGuard ignores. This has important implications for toxicity research. Reporting results from a single evaluator can be misleading. A method that appears successful under one evaluator may fail under another. We recommend using multiple evaluators with different design philosophies to obtain a complete picture of model behavior changes. Inference : Safety evaluators disagree—LlamaGuard and PolyGuard often report opposite effects, revealing they measure fundamentally different behaviors.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: This work demonstrates that toxic outputs in language models can be effectively mitigated by detecting and modifying a small set of specialized neural pathways. Both deactivation and dampening achieve mean toxicity reduction of 25% across diverse model scales. We find that larger models are more amenable to targeted intervention, suggesting that toxic knowledge is localized rather than distributed. Selecting the top-5 toxic paths by activation ratio proves sufficient for substantial toxicity reduction without comprehensive model retraining. Future work should explore architecture-specific optimization strategies and measure downstream impacts on model helpfulness and factuality. This approach offers a practical path toward safer language models through interpretable neural interventions. These findings highlight that effective detoxification requires component-aware editing, conservative hyperparameters, and evaluation across multiple safety benchmarks.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Our method operates in a strictly inference-only, parameter-frozen setting, and therefore does not capture toxicity mitigation achievable through fine-tuning, LoRA, or RLHF. Toxicity localization is derived from mean activation differences over a fixed subset of prompts, which may underrepresent rare, long-range, or highly contextual toxic behaviors. Although our experiments focus on decoder-only models, the core methodology—activation collection, component-wise scoring, and inference-time scaling—is architecture-agnostic in principle. Adapting the framework to other architectures (e.g., encoder–decoder models or mixture-of-experts) would require identifying corresponding attention and feed-forward modules and appropriately placing forward hooks, without altering the underlying detection or intervention logic. Finally, our evaluation relies on automated safety classifiers, such as PolyGuard and LLaMA-Guard, which may introduce bias or misclassification; we do not include human judgments.

sections.heading: Ethics
sections.text: This work focuses on analyzing and mitigating toxic behavior in language models using inference-time, non-invasive interventions that do not require retraining or the deployment of new models. All experiments are conducted on publicly available datasets containing potentially harmful language, which are used solely for research purposes and never redistributed. While the proposed method aims to reduce harmful outputs, automated toxicity evaluators may reflect existing biases; therefore, our results should not be interpreted as a complete guarantee of safety. We emphasize that this work is intended to support safer model behavior and informed deployment, not to enable misuse or censorship. We acknolwedge the use of AI assistants to help rewrite the content to improve readability and writing.

sections.heading: Meow2X
sections.text: All experiments are conducted in a parameter-frozen setting on the language generation task. In contrast to fine-tuning-based approaches (e.g., LoRA), no weight updates or optimization steps are performed . All interventions operate solely at inference time via activation-level scaling of selected model components. We perform a controlled hyperparameter search over the intervention space, varying the number of selected layers K ∈ { 5 , 10 } K\in\{5,10\} , deactivation strength α ∈ { 0.3 , 0.5 } \alpha\in\{0.3,0.5\} , and layer selection strategy ( Top-K ranking vs. dynamic thresholding based on activation statistics). Interventions are applied to three component scopes: MLP-only , attention-only , and joint (MLP+attention). Our experimental setup spans five pretrained instruction-tuned LLMs and two toxicity benchmarks , yielding a total of 90 configurations : 5 5 models × \times 2 2 datasets × \times 3 3 component scopes × \times 3 3 intervention techniques ( deactivation , dampening , and adaptive scaling ). Each configuration is evaluated on 5,000 5{,}000 prompts per dataset ( 2,500 2{,}500 toxic and 2,500 2{,}500 neutral). Toxicity is assessed using two independent evaluators— LlamaGuard and PolyGuard —while generation quality is monitored via perplexity. All experiments are executed in FP16 inference mode on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU.

sections.heading: TRNE
sections.text: The dataset consists of 5000 toxic-neutral pairs from ParaDetox Logacheva et al. (2022) , where 1000 samples are for localization, and 2000 are for activation collection. Hyperparameters K = 5 K=5 (top layers), α ∈ [ 1.0 , 5.0 ] \alpha\in[1.0,5.0] , γ = 0.1 \gamma=0.1 , ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} . We evaluate the toxicity using: LlamaGuard-3-8B (8-bit quantized) ( Dubey et al., 2024 ) and PolyGuard-Qwen-Smol ( Kumar et al., 2025 ) to capture different dimensions learnt by the classifiers. For Fluency, we utilise: WikiText-2 perplexity (500 samples). Generations were computed as: 50 tokens, temperature=0.7, top- p p =0.9.

Mechanistic Localization and Targeted Suppression in Language Models WARNING: The content contains offensive model outputs and is toxic. Himanshu Beniwal Affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar Mayank Singh Affiliation: {himanshubeniwal, singh.mayank}@iitgn.ac.in Abstract Large language models frequently generate toxic, hateful, or harmful content, yet existing mitigation methods rely on costly retraining or output-level filtering with no mechanistic insight into where toxicity originates internally. We introduce Meow2X and TRNE , two complementary retraining-free frameworks that localize toxicity to specific layers and neurons by analyzing activation differentials between toxic and neutral prompts, then suppress them via inference-time scaling or minimal rank-one weight edits—without any gradient descent. Evaluations across five LMs, two benchmarks, and 90 configurations using dual safety evaluators demonstrate consistent toxicity reduction while preserving language modeling quality. Our analysis reveals that toxicity is disproportionately encoded in early MLP layers, varies across architectures, and is systematically underestimated by single-evaluator setups—underscoring the need for multi-evaluator safety assessment. By bridging mechanistic interpretability with practical detoxification, our framework offers a principled path toward safer, more transparent language models. Code is available at this URL 1 1 1 https://github.com/himanshubeniwal/Toxicity-Mitigation . 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across various downstream tasks; however, their propensity to generate toxic, hateful, or harmful content remains a significant challenge for real-world deployment ( Sap et al., 2019a ; Gehman et al., 2020 ; Dementieva et al., 2025 ; Welbl et al., 2021 ; Hui et al., 2024 ) . Existing safety mechanisms—including instruction tuning, RLHF, and adversarial fine-tuning—typically require expensive retraining or exhibit limited transfer to out-of-distribution inputs ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Beniwal et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . We address this with two complementary post-hoc methods that localize and suppress toxic neural components without retraining, exploiting the observation that toxicity correlates with specific activation patterns in attention and MLP modules ( Meng et al., 2022 ; Zhang and Nanda, 2023 ; Costa-jussà et al., 2024 ; Shaik et al., 2025 ) . Figure 1: Overview of the Meow2X framework. Given toxic and neutral prompts, the model identifies toxic layers (attn-5, MLP-17) via activation differentials. Three inference-time suppression strategies reduce toxic generation while preserving neutral outputs, without any parameter updates. Research Gap Prior work has identified toxic neurons and suppressed them ( Suau et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) , but typically targets individual neurons or fixed concepts without systematically selecting layers per model and dataset ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zhao and Huang, 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025b ) . Most methods also apply generic damping rather than interventions tailored to the difference between toxic and neutral inputs ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Villate-Castillo et al., 2024 ; Pozzobon et al., 2024 ; Siu et al., 2025 ) . There is no simple, data-driven algorithm that (1) detects which layers are most correlated with toxicity and (2) suppresses them while tracking output quality ( Koh et al., 2024 ; Suau et al., 2024 ) . We fill this gap with Meow2X ( M echanistic E xploration o f W eight-level To x icity), a parameter-frozen inference-time framework based on activation differentials, and TRNE ( T oxicity R eduction via N euron E diting), a lightweight rank-one weight update guided by contrastive gradient localization. Motivation Both methods share the insight that only a small fraction of layers govern toxic behavior ( Lee et al., 2025 ) . As shown in Figure 1 , Meow2X identifies these layers via mean activation differences between toxic and neutral inputs and suppresses them at inference time via scaling—leaving weights unchanged and the intervention fully reversible ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Shaik et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . TRNE localizes the same layers via contrastive gradient norms and commits a minimal, norm-constrained rank-one weight edit that encodes the toxic direction directly into the projection matrix—offering a persistent correction without gradient descent. Together, they combine interpretability (knowing where toxicity arises) with effectiveness (measured by safety classifiers) ( Neplenbroek et al., 2024 ; Jain et al., 2024 ) , grounded in mechanistic interpretability findings that toxic behaviors are mediated by localized neuron-level circuits ( Olah et al., 2020 ; Meng et al., 2022 ; Geiger et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., ) . Contributions Our contributions are threefold: • A principled toxic layer detection framework using activation differentials ( Meow2X ) and contrastive gradient norms ( TRNE ), revealing where toxicity is encoded in language models. • A controlled evaluation across 90 configurations —five LLMs, two datasets, three component scopes, three intervention strategies—without any parameter updates for Meow2X and with minimal rank-one edits for TRNE . • A model-agnostic detoxification pipeline that preserves language modeling capability via reversible inference-time scaling ( Meow2X ) or norm-constrained weight editing ( TRNE ). Algorithm 1 Toxic Layer Detection and Mitigation 1: Pretrained model M M , toxic prompts 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , neutral prompts 𝒩 \mathcal{N} , component c ∈ { MLP, Attn, Both } c\in\{\text{MLP, Attn, Both}\} 2: Mitigated model M ~ \tilde{M} 3: Compute mean activations μ t ℓ \mu_{t}^{\ell} and μ n ℓ \mu_{n}^{\ell} for each layer ℓ \ell 4: Compute activation shift Δ ℓ = μ t ℓ − μ n ℓ \Delta^{\ell}=\mu_{t}^{\ell}-\mu_{n}^{\ell} 5: Compute layer score S ℓ = ∑ | Δ ℓ | S^{\ell}=\sum|\Delta^{\ell}| 6: Compute neuron contribution c ℓ c^{\ell} via high-magnitude activations 7: Select toxic layers ℒ \mathcal{L} using Top- k k or dynamic thresholding 8: Apply mitigation with scaling factor α ℓ \alpha^{\ell} to ℓ ∈ ℒ \ell\in\mathcal{L} 9: Evaluate toxicity reduction and perplexity with two evaluators. 10: return M ~ \tilde{M} and evaluation metrics 2 Related Work Detoxification of Language Models. Prior work on toxicity mitigation in language models has largely focused on training-time interventions, including supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning from human feedback, as well as on output-level filtering and rejection sampling ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Beniwal et al., 2025 ; Sap et al., 2019b ) . While effective at reducing harmful generations, these approaches treat toxicity as a surface-level behavior and provide limited insight into how such behaviors arise internally ( Dathathri et al., 2019 ) . Moreover, they typically require retraining or additional inference-time classifiers ( Costa-jussà et al., 2024 ) . In contrast, our work operates directly on internal representations and performs targeted inference-time interventions without modifying model parameters. Interpretability via Internal Representations. Mechanistic interpretability research has shown that neural behaviors can often be localized to specific layers, neurons, or substructures ( Zhang and Nanda, 2023 ) . Methods such as Network Dissection ( Bau et al., 2017 ) and representational similarity analysis ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) demonstrate that internal activations encode semantically meaningful features and that behaviors can be traced to localized components. These findings motivate our approach, which explicitly compares mean activations induced by toxic and neutral inputs to identify layers and neurons that disproportionately contribute to toxic behavior ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Siu et al., 2025 ) . Targeted and Causal Interventions. Recent studies have explored the causal manipulation of internal components through neuron ablation, attention head suppression, or feature scaling, demonstrating that selective intervention can reliably alter model outputs ( Li and Janson, 2024 ; Dai et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . However, many such approaches rely on manual selection or task-specific heuristics. Our method systematizes this process by using activation differentials and contribution-based scoring to automatically identify toxic layers and apply controlled scaling through forward hooks, enabling reproducible and architecture-agnostic intervention ( Rai et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Evaluation and Positioning. Unlike prior detoxification methods that rely on a single evaluator or aggregate metrics, our framework employs multiple independent safety classifiers and jointly measures toxicity reduction and language modeling quality ( Yang et al., 2025a ; Dutta, 2024 ) . Overall, our work bridges safety and interpretability by framing toxicity as an internal representational phenomenon ( Suau et al., 2024 ) . Rather than only suppressing harmful outputs, we focus on revealing where toxicity is encoded within the model, providing both practical mitigation and mechanistic insight into models. Positioning Against Baselines. We position our work relative to the closest prior methods: Whispering Experts Suau et al. (2024) suppresses toxic neurons but requires task-specific expert identification and does not generalize across architectures without per-model re-identification. SafeEdit Wang et al. (2024) applies knowledge editing via gradient-based updates but requires backpropagation at inference time. DExperts Liu et al. (2021) and PPLM Dathathri et al. (2020) are output-level steering methods that cannot localize toxicity to specific model components. Unlike all of the above, Meow2X operates without any parameter updates, backpropagation, or expert model, making it strictly lighter at inference time. A full quantitative comparison is left to future work as it requires standardizing generation hyperparameters, decoding strategies, and evaluation prompts across codebases—a non-trivial engineering challenge acknowledged by prior surveys Villate-Castillo et al. (2024) . 3 Methodology - Meow2X As highlighted in Algorithm 1 , we explain the operations as: 3.1 Toxic Layer Detection We identify toxic layers by analyzing systematic differences in internal activations elicited by toxic and neutral inputs. Given a pretrained language model M M with L L model layers, we focus on either attention blocks, MLP blocks, or both, depending on the experimental setting. Activation Collection. Let 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} and 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}_{n} denote sets of toxic and neutral prompts, respectively. For each layer ℓ \ell , we collect mean activation vectors by registering forward hooks during inference and averaging hidden states across tokens and batch samples. We compute separate mean activations for toxic inputs μ t ℓ \mu_{t}^{\ell} and neutral inputs μ n ℓ \mu_{n}^{\ell} using batched forward passes to ensure stable estimates. Activation Differentials and Layer Scoring. To quantify toxicity-specific behavior, we compute the activation differential Δ ℓ = μ t ℓ − μ n ℓ \Delta^{\ell}=\mu_{t}^{\ell}-\mu_{n}^{\ell} for each layer. We assign a scalar toxicity score to each layer by aggregating absolute differences across neurons, S ℓ = ‖ Δ ℓ ‖ 1 , S^{\ell}=\|\Delta^{\ell}\|_{1}, where higher values indicate stronger representational divergence induced by toxic prompts. This score provides a coarse but robust signal for ranking layers by toxicity relevance. Neuron-Level Contribution Analysis. Beyond layer-level scoring, we estimate the concentration of toxicity within a layer. For each Δ ℓ \Delta^{\ell} , we identify toxic neurons as those whose absolute activation difference exceeds the 90 th 90^{\text{th}} percentile. We then compute a contribution ratio c ℓ = ∑ i ∈ 𝒯 ℓ | Δ i ℓ | ∑ i | Δ i ℓ | , c^{\ell}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}_{\ell}}|\Delta^{\ell}_{i}|}{\sum_{i}|\Delta^{\ell}_{i}|}, where 𝒯 ℓ \mathcal{T}_{\ell} denotes the set of toxic neurons in layer ℓ \ell . This captures whether toxicity arises from a small subset of highly influential neurons or is diffusely distributed. Layer Selection. We select toxic layers using either a Top- k k strategy, which chooses the k k layers with the highest S ℓ S^{\ell} , or a dynamic thresholding strategy. In the latter, layers are selected if their score exceeds a data-dependent threshold defined by the mean and standard deviation of { S ℓ } \{S^{\ell}\} , with safeguards in place to enforce minimum and maximum numbers of selected layers. Both strategies operate identically across model architectures and component types. Outputs. The detector returns (i) the set of selected toxic layers, (ii) layer-wise toxicity scores S ℓ S^{\ell} , and (iii) neuron-level contribution statistics c ℓ c^{\ell} . These signals are subsequently used to guide targeted inference-time interventions while preserving the original model parameters. 3.2 Layer Deactivation Mitigation Strategies. Following toxic layer identification, we intervene directly at inference time by modifying intermediate activations of selected model components. Let ℒ \mathcal{L} denote the set of detected toxic layers. For each layer ℓ ∈ ℒ \ell\in\mathcal{L} , we register forward hooks that rescale the output activations of either the attention block, the MLP block, or both, depending on the experimental setting. These interventions are lightweight, do not alter model parameters, and can be removed after generation. 3.2.1 Deactivation The deactivation strategy applies uniform suppression to all selected layers. For each ℓ ∈ ℒ \ell\in\mathcal{L} , the layer output is multiplied by a constant scaling factor α = 1 − s \alpha=1-s , where s ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] s\in(0,1] is the deactivation strength. This strategy aggressively attenuates toxic representations by uniformly reducing their contribution to downstream layers. To avoid destabilizing the forward pass, the scaling factor is clipped to a minimum value α min \alpha_{\min} , ensuring that information flow is preserved. 3.2.2 Dampening The dampening strategy performs moderate suppression by applying a reduced scaling factor relative to deactivation. Instead of fully applying the specified strength, activations are scaled by α = 1 − s 2 \alpha=1-\frac{s}{2} , resulting in a smoother attenuation of toxic signals. This strategy is particularly effective when toxicity is distributed across multiple layers and excessive suppression may harm fluency or coherence. 3.2.3 Adaptive Scaling The adaptive strategy introduces contribution-aware suppression by conditioning the scaling factor on each layer’s estimated toxicity contribution. For a layer ℓ \ell , the scaling factor is computed as α ℓ = 1 − s ⋅ c ℓ max ℓ ′ ∈ ℒ ⁡ c ℓ ′ \alpha_{\ell}=1-s\cdot\frac{c_{\ell}}{\max_{\ell^{\prime}\in\mathcal{L}}c_{\ell^{\prime}}} , where c ℓ c_{\ell} denotes the normalized contribution score derived from high-magnitude activation differences. Layers with stronger toxic influence are thus suppressed more aggressively, while layers with weaker contributions remain largely intact. As with other strategies, α ℓ \alpha_{\ell} is lower-bounded by α min \alpha_{\min} to maintain numerical stability. Practical Considerations All mitigation strategies are applied only during generation and are removed immediately afterward, preserving the original model for subsequent evaluations. The approach is fully model-agnostic, supports attention-only, MLP-only, or combined interventions, and integrates seamlessly with both top- k k and dynamic threshold–based layer selection. Figure 3: The layer analysis for Qwen2.5 over the ParaDetox dataset. Here we show the (top-left) toxicity scores per layer, (top-right) contribution by layers, (bottom-left) component vs toxicity score, and (bottom-right) toxicity score vs contribution score. Takeaway : Toxicity is more observed in the MLPs of initial layers and last layers . 4 Methodology - TRNE 4.1 Method Description 4.1.1 Contrastive Gradient Localization For each input x x , we backpropagate through − ℒ ent ​ ( x ) -\mathcal{L}_{\text{ent}}(x) and register backward hooks on target modules to capture gradient norms. Layers where toxic inputs elicit substantially stronger gradients than neutral inputs are selected as toxic regions. 4.1.2 Pre-Projection Activation Collection At each selected hotspot layer l l , we register forward hooks on the output projection (attention: o_proj ; MLP: down_proj ) to capture input activations at the last token position, ϕ l ​ ( x ) = h l ( last ) ​ ( x ) ∈ ℝ d in \phi_{l}(x)=h_{l}^{(\text{last})}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}} . Mean activations μ T \mu_{T} and μ N \mu_{N} are computed over the toxic and neutral sets respectively; the difference δ = μ T − μ N \delta=\mu_{T}-\mu_{N} defines the toxic direction at that layer. 4.1.3 Rank-One Weight Update The key formula modifies the weight matrix: W new = W − α × torch.outer ​ ( δ , μ T ) ‖ μ T ‖ 2 + ϵ W_{\text{new}}=W-\alpha\times\frac{\texttt{torch.outer}(\delta,\mu_{T})}{\|\mu_{T}\|^{2}+\epsilon} This creates a “detector” ( μ T \mu_{T} ) and a “correction” ( δ \delta ). When future input looks toxic (similar to μ T \mu_{T} ), the matrix automatically subtracts the toxic direction. Neutral inputs (orthogonal to μ T \mu_{T} ) pass through unchanged. Analogy : Like calibrating a speaker system. You identify which frequencies cause distortion (localization), measure the distortion pattern (activation collection), then adjust the equalizer to cancel exactly that distortion without affecting clean frequencies (rank-one update). 5 Experimental Settings 5.1 Dataset We evaluate our framework on two complementary toxicity benchmarks with distinct structural properties. We evaluate on: Real Toxicity Prompts (RTP) 2 2 2 https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/real-toxicity-prompts ( Gehman et al., 2020 ) and ParaDetox 3 3 3 https://huggingface.co/datasets/textdetox/multilingual_paradetox ( Logacheva et al., 2022 ; Dementieva et al., 2021 ) . Let 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} and 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}_{n} denote toxic and neutral prompt sets, respectively. For RTP, prompts with toxicity score τ ≥ 0.5 \tau\geq 0.5 are assigned to 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{t} , and the rest to 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}_{n} . ParaDetox provides paired samples ( x t , x n ) (x_{t},x_{n}) that differ primarily in toxicity while preserving semantics. We sample | 𝒟 t | = | 𝒟 n | = 2500 |\mathcal{D}_{t}|=|\mathcal{D}_{n}|=2500 , truncate inputs to 512 tokens, and cache all samples to ensure reproducibility. More details in Section § A.1 . 5.2 Models Experiments are conducted on instruction-tuned causal language models M θ M_{\theta} in the 1B–3B parameter range, including Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct , gemma-2-2b-it , Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct , phi-2 , and TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 variants. Each model consists of a stack of layers { ℓ 1 , … , ℓ L } \{\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{L}\} , where each layer contains an attention block ℓ attn \ell^{\text{attn}} and an MLP block ℓ mlp \ell^{\text{mlp}} . The pipeline explicitly supports heterogeneous architectural layouts by dynamically identifying blocks across model families (e.g., model.layers, transformer.h, or attn.k). Our analysis is performed on attention-only, MLP-only, and combined components. All models are evaluated in inference mode using half-precision weights, without retraining or parameter updates, and batch sizes are tuned per model for stable activation collection. 5.3 Toxicity Detection Toxicity is evaluated using two independent safety classifiers, Llama-Guard-3-8B ( Dubey et al., 2024 ) and PolyGuard-Qwen ( Kumar et al., 2025 ) . Given a prompt–response pair ( x , y ) (x,y) , each evaluator outputs a binary unsafe indicator u ∈ { 0 , 1 } u\in\{0,1\} and a set of violated safety categories 𝒞 ⊆ { S 1 , … , S 14 } \mathcal{C}\subseteq\{S_{1},\ldots,S_{14}\} . The categories cover violence, hate, sexual content, self-harm, privacy violations, and related safety risks. Using two heterogeneous evaluators enables robust verification of toxicity reductions across category boundaries. More details in Appendix A.1 . 5.4 Metrics The effectiveness of detoxification is measured by comparing aggregate toxicity rates before and after mitigation. Let U before U_{\text{before}} and U after U_{\text{after}} denote the fraction of unsafe generations; toxicity reduction is defined as Δ ​ U = U before − U after \Delta U=U_{\text{before}}-U_{\text{after}} . Model utility is assessed via perplexity (PPL), computed using teacher-forced likelihood with attention-mask weighting. In addition, we report layer-level toxicity scores S ℓ S^{\ell} , neuron contribution ratios c ℓ c^{\ell} , and applied scaling factors α ℓ \alpha^{\ell} to analyze safety–utility trade-offs at a mechanistic level. 6 Results (RQ1) Can toxicity be localized to specific layers and neurons using activation differences? Meow2X Figures 2 – 4 jointly provide a multi-resolution view of how toxicity is encoded within Qwen-2.5 across layers, components, and neurons on the ParaDetox dataset. The neuron-level heatmaps (Figure 2 ) show that toxicity-related activation differences are sparse and structured rather than uniformly distributed (We observed different patterns in different models; see appendix § A.3 for more details), with particularly strong signals concentrated in the initial MLP layers (layers 1–5). This pattern is further corroborated by the layer-wise toxicity scores and contribution plots (Figure 3 ), where MLP components consistently exhibit higher toxicity scores S = ∥ Δ ∥ 1 S=\lVert\Delta\rVert_{1} than attention across both early and late layers, while attention contributions remain comparatively stable and lower in magnitude. The box plots and scatter analyses reveal a clear separation between MLP and attention components, indicating that toxicity is disproportionately encoded in feed-forward transformations. Finally, the neuron-level grids (Figure 4 ) demonstrate that within high-scoring MLP layers, toxicity is dominated by a small subset of neurons exhibiting large activation deviations beyond the percentile threshold. While TRNE achieves toxicity reduction on Llama-family models with moderate edit strength and few layers, aggressive hyperparameters can catastrophically degrade model quality. On Gemma-2-2B-it with high edit strength (20) and many layers (10), MLP editing caused perplexity to explode from 29.9 to 1744.6, rendering the model incoherent (As shown in Figures 14 , 15 , and 16 ). Simultaneously, toxicity increased by 21 percentage points on PolyGuard—the opposite of the intended effect. This fragility stems from the cumulative nature of weight updates: each layer modification compounds across multiple layers. When the total perturbation exceeds the model’s tolerance, coherent generation collapses. We recommend low-to-moderate edit strength (1 to 5) and editing only 3 to 5 layers as safe operating ranges, with architecture-specific tuning for non-Llama models. Finding : Weight editing is fragile—high edit strength or too many layers causes model collapse with perplexity exploding. (RQ5) Safety Evaluators Measure Different Aspects of Model Behavior? LlamaGuard and PolyGuard produce dramatically different toxicity assessments on identical outputs. Baseline measurements differ by 25 to 40 percentage points, with PolyGuard consistently detecting far more toxic content. More critically, the evaluators disagree on the effect of attention editing: LlamaGuard reports improvement while PolyGuard reports degradation. This disagreement reveals that the evaluators measure fundamentally different phenomena. LlamaGuard focuses on explicitly harmful content generation, while PolyGuard additionally penalizes refusal behavior and evasive responses. When attention layers are edited, models may become more likely to refuse requests, which PolyGuard considers problematic, but LlamaGuard ignores. This has important implications for toxicity research. Reporting results from a single evaluator can be misleading. A method that appears successful under one evaluator may fail under another. We recommend using multiple evaluators with different design philosophies to obtain a complete picture of model behavior changes. Inference : Safety evaluators disagree—LlamaGuard and PolyGuard often report opposite effects, revealing they measure fundamentally different behaviors. 7 Conclusion This work demonstrates that toxic outputs in language models can be effectively mitigated by detecting and modifying a small set of specialized neural pathways. Both deactivation and dampening achieve mean toxicity reduction of 25% across diverse model scales. We find that larger models are more amenable to targeted intervention, suggesting that toxic knowledge is localized rather than distributed. Selecting the top-5 toxic paths by activation ratio proves sufficient for substantial toxicity reduction without comprehensive model retraining. Future work should explore architecture-specific optimization strategies and measure downstream impacts on model helpfulness and factuality. This approach offers a practical path toward safer language models through interpretable neural interventions. These findings highlight that effective detoxification requires component-aware editing, conservative hyperparameters, and evaluation across multiple safety benchmarks. Limitations Our method operates in a strictly inference-only, parameter-frozen setting, and therefore does not capture toxicity mitigation achievable through fine-tuning, LoRA, or RLHF. Toxicity localization is derived from mean activation differences over a fixed subset of prompts, which may underrepresent rare, long-range, or highly contextual toxic behaviors. Although our experiments focus on decoder-only models, the core methodology—activation collection, component-wise scoring, and inference-time scaling—is architecture-agnostic in principle. Adapting the framework to other architectures (e.g., encoder–decoder models or mixture-of-experts) would require identifying corresponding attention and feed-forward modules and appropriately placing forward hooks, without altering the underlying detection or intervention logic. Finally, our evaluation relies on automated safety classifiers, such as PolyGuard and LLaMA-Guard, which may introduce bias or misclassification; we do not include human judgments. Ethics This work focuses on analyzing and mitigating toxic behavior in language models using inference-time, non-invasive interventions that do not require retraining or the deployment of new models. All experiments are conducted on publicly available datasets containing potentially harmful language, which are used solely for research purposes and never redistributed. While the proposed method aims to reduce harmful outputs, automated toxicity evaluators may reflect existing biases; therefore, our results should not be interpreted as a complete guarantee of safety. We emphasize that this work is intended to support safer model behavior and informed deployment, not to enable misuse or censorship.
